read: full: abstract, sections 1-6 (pp. 1-8, proceedings pp. 404-411) in full; appendices A (limitations), B (Cohen's kappa), F (metrics), G-K (guidelines, costs, sample reliability, base vs chat) read; prompt and score appendices skimmed
venue_now: GEM2 2025, Fourth Workshop on Generation, Evaluation and Metrics, ACL, pp. 404-430, 31 July-1 August 2025 (page 1 footer; arXiv 2406.12624v6, 18 Aug 2025)
what_it_is: A meta-evaluation of LLM judges in a deliberately clean setting: judges see a TriviaQA question, its reference answers and an exam-taker model's answer, and reply 'correct' or 'incorrect', following the same guidelines as the human annotators. Eleven LLM judges (Llama-2/3/3.1 sizes, Gemma 2B, Mistral 7B, JudgeLM 7B, GPT-4 Turbo) and two lexical baselines (exact match, contains) grade nine exam-taker models on 400 questions, against human labels whose inter-annotator Scott's pi is 96.2. Only the largest judges reach Scott's pi in the high 80s, still about 8 points below humans, and their benchmark scores can differ from the human scores by up to 5 points; percent agreement barely separates judges and can hide 10-20 point score gaps. Error analysis finds leniency, trouble with under-specified answers, prompt sensitivity, and some judges passing dummy answers such as 'Yes'.
domain: open-domain factual QA (TriviaQA); no technical or reasoning content
size: 400 TriviaQA questions x 9 exam-taker models (Llama-2 7B/13B/70B base and chat, Mistral 7B base and chat, GPT-4 Turbo); 11 LLM judges plus 2 lexical baselines (13 'judges'); 1,200 answers triple-annotated for inter-human agreement
source_of_items: existing benchmark (TriviaQA unfiltered validation set, questions from trivia and quiz-league websites), with answers generated by the exam-taker models
evaluation: LLM judge giving a binary correct/incorrect verdict with reference answers, compared with human labels by percent agreement, Scott's pi, score deviation, Spearman rank correlation of exam-taker rankings, precision and recall, and a leniency model
human_validation: CS graduate students annotated every exam-taker answer; three annotators on 1,200 answers (600 from Llama2 7B, 600 from Llama3.1 70B) agreed with the majority at Scott's pi 96.2 +/- 1.07 and 98.52% +/- 0.42% (p. 5; p. 13; p. 18); thereafter one human label per answer. A 900-output manual error analysis of Llama-7B Base answers (p. 6).

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate, not cited in the May paper. It is the batch's closest analogue to EngTrace's residual judge: a binary correct/incorrect verdict given a reference, which is what E5 does on milestones the deterministic check missed (REACHED or not, given the gold value). Its findings bear on EngTrace in three ways. (1) Even with a reference and near-perfect human agreement, the best judges stay below human agreement and are lenient: well-aligned judges make more false positives than false negatives, and most judges' leniency P+ is well above 0.5 (Figure 3b p. 5; p. 8); the writers can set this against E5's own precision 0.930 and recall 0.989 on milestones. (2) Percent agreement hides large score errors and rank correlation is not score accuracy (contains and Mistral 7B reach rho 0.99 and 0.98 while scoring far from humans, p. 6), which is the case against the May paper's single Spearman rho = 0.632 and for reporting chance-corrected agreement and per-class errors against the 15 experts, as the new validation does. (3) Under-specified (partial) answers are the hardest case, with recall 33.9% for GPT-4 Turbo (Table 2, p. 7), relevant to partial milestones and the 0.5 partial-credit answer class.

suggested_wording: Even when judging short answers against a reference, a setting with near-perfect human agreement, the best LLM judges fall short of inter-human agreement, are lenient, and can match percent agreement or model rankings while misestimating scores, so judge validation needs chance-corrected agreement and error rates against human labels (Thakur et al., 2025).
facts_to_cite: 11 LLM judges and 2 lexical baselines grade 9 exam-taker models on 400 TriviaQA questions with reference answers, replying only 'correct' or 'incorrect' (pp. 2-4).
Human annotators agree almost perfectly in this setting: Scott's pi 96.2 +/- 1.07, percent agreement 98.52% (p. 5).
Only GPT-4 Turbo, Llama-3 70B and Llama-3.1 70B reach Scott's pi in the high 80s; the best (Llama-3 70B) is 8 points behind human agreement (p. 5, Figure 1b p. 2).
Judges with Scott's pi above 80 still differ by up to 5 points from human-assigned scores; judges with over 90% percent agreement can differ by more than 10 points (p. 6; 10-20 points, p. 2).

Percent agreement barely discriminates between judges; the authors recommend Scott's pi alongside percent agreement and qualitative analysis (pp. 5, 8). An earlier version used Cohen's kappa, replaced over its theoretical issues (p. 4 footnote 2; appendix B pp. 13-14).
High rank correlation is not score accuracy: contains and Mistral 7B rank exam-takers with rho 0.99 and 0.98 while assigning divergent scores (p. 6).
Well-aligned judges produce more false positives than false negatives, and most judges show a leniency bias (P+ significantly above 0.5) (Figure 3b p. 5; p. 8).
Under-specified answers are hard to catch: recall 33.9% for GPT-4 Turbo and 23.3% for Llama-3 70B (Table 2, p. 7).
Some judges mark dummy answers ('Yes', 'Sure') correct, and judges do not always accept a verbatim reference answer (Figure 5, pp. 7-8).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: reference-guided binary correctness verdicts by an LLM judge (E5's task on residual milestones), validation against human labels with chance-corrected agreement, per-class error analysis, and a deterministic baseline (exact match, contains) beside the judge. Lacks: generated instances, gold traces, step-level evaluation, engineering or any technical content (trivia answers), domain-expert validators (CS graduate students), and any test of judge-candidate relatedness.
notes: Paragraph: process supervision and judge validity. Recommended should rather than must: it is the cleanest support for how EngTrace validates its judge (chance-corrected agreement and error rates against humans, not percent agreement or a rank correlation) and for judge leniency, but it is a workshop paper on trivia QA and a reviewer is unlikely to name it specifically. Counting note: the abstract's 'thirteen models' as judges includes the two lexical baselines; appendix A says 11 LLMs (p. 13). The search note is accurate; its 'Cohen's kappa in an earlier version' is confirmed (p. 4 footnote 2).
